tldr: We propose MAWAM, a world model that jointly generates the entire team's future visual changes and executable control actions in a single sample, achieving an average success rate of 67.8% (+18.9 percentage points over prior methods) across two-robot real-world coordinated tasks.
hero_caption: Overview of the MAWAM training and inference pipeline. Starting from a pretrained single-robot backbone, it undergoes single-robot warm-up and then jointly predicts and generates camera views, states, and actions across the team using cross-agent attention.
overview:
When multiple robots collaborate on a single task, one robot's movement alters the shared environment, directly impacting its teammate's actions and field of view. For instance, one robot cannot drop clothes into a laundry bag unless the other robot opens and holds it up. To succeed in such tightly coordinated tasks, visually anticipating how the physical world will change through joint actions is indispensable.

However, existing multi-robot control methods either run policies independently or rely on high-level language or trajectory planning, failing to directly predict visual outcomes in the physical world. On the other hand, while video-generation world models can predict future scenes, they cannot output control signals to drive real robots.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates future camera views and executable control action chunks across all robots in a single sampling step. Built on a single-robot foundation model, it incorporates cross-agent attention to attend to teammate representations, alongside decoupled representations for specific cameras, joints, and task roles.

Evaluated on challenging tasks with two real-world bimanual mobile robots (using only six onboard camera views and no static overhead cameras) and simulation tasks with up to four arms, MAWAM achieved a 67.8% average success rate on real hardware and 90.3% in simulation, significantly outperforming existing VLA baselines.
contributions: Proposed MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly denoises and generates future camera views and continuous actions for the entire team in a single sample.
Designed regular-simplex rotary position embeddings and task-role representations that preserve robot-specific view-state-action correspondences while flexibly assigning operational roles.
Constructed a two-stage training framework that smoothly adapts from single-robot warm-up to synchronized team-stage learning.
Demonstrated state-of-the-art coordination performance on two real robots across six onboard views without overhead cameras, and on eight simulation tasks with up to four arms.

sections.heading: Why does multi-robot coordination require predicting the physical future?
sections.summary: When robots cooperate in the physical world, one's action dictates the other's operating environment. This section introduces a new formulation: a multi-agent world model that jointly predicts the physical future and team actions.
sections.details:
When robots work as a team in homes or factories, they must perform tightly coordinated tasks such as object handovers, folding deformable cloth, or carrying heavy objects together. Crucially, while each robot observes the world from its own perspective, one robot's movements continuously reshape the shared environment and constrain its partner's next move in real time.

Existing coordination approaches face three main challenges:
- Decentralized policies: Running separate policies per robot leads to coordination drift, resulting in idling or oscillatory, stuttering motions.
- Trajectory and action generation: While they can coordinate multi-robot trajectories, they fail to anticipate the visual consequences on the environment.
- Language and logic-guided approaches: Relying on high-level planning via LLMs struggles to capture fine-grained physical changes in the world.

Furthermore, recent video-generation world models synthesize high-fidelity future frames, but they only consume control inputs rather than driving the robot directly. To overcome this, this work extends single-robot world models into MAWAM, denoising all agents' actions and future camera views inside a single Transformer. Through unique representations that avoid mixing up individual cameras and control interfaces, along with a two-stage training strategy, MAWAM realizes sophisticated coordination without overhead cameras.

sections.heading: At the intersection of coordination, multi-agent world models, and action generation
sections.summary: This section reviews three research lines—cooperative robot control, multi-view world prediction, and world-action models—and explains how MAWAM unifies them.
sections.details:
This work stands at the intersection of three active research trends:

### Multi-Robot Action Coordination
Decentralized methods align representations across individual policies (such as MIMIC-D or CLS-DP), diffusion models jointly generate multi-agent trajectories (such as MADiff), and other methods leverage LLM dialogues or temporal logic (such as RoCo, LTLDiff, and MA-VLA). However, these focus solely on action coordination and do not directly generate the visual consequences of the team's actions.

### Shared World Prediction
Methods reconstructing shared states from egocentric cameras and multi-view consistent video generation models (such as Solaris and MultiWorld) are advancing rapidly. Yet, these operate as forward simulators predicting how the world changes given actions, rather than deployable action policies in the real world.

### Action Learning with Visual Futures
In single-robot domains, world-action models (such as DreamZero and Fast-WAM) leverage future visual prediction representations for action generation, showing strong control capabilities. MAWAM extends this paradigm to multi-agent coordination for the first time. The defining difference is coupling partner actions, ego actions, and the resulting team-wide future views into a single unified generative process.

sections.heading: Architecture and training: Weaving actions and future views together
sections.summary: MAWAM processes tokens from all agents through a single Transformer, jointly generating future videos and action chunks via cross-agent attention. Regular-simplex agent IDs and role embeddings prevent confusion while enabling flexible coordination.
sections.details:
The core of MAWAM lies in its unified team prediction model and its representation design that preserves separate control interfaces for each robot.

### 3.1 Predicting Joint Actions and Outcomes
Consider $N$ robots operating in a shared space. Each robot $i$ has its own state $\mathbf{s}^i_t$, assigned role $r_i$, and a set of onboard cameras $\mathcal{V}_i$. MAWAM takes these as input and jointly generates continuous action chunks $\mathbf{u}^i_t$ over the next 24 steps (1.2 seconds in simulation, 1.6 seconds on real hardware) along with 8 future camera frames across all robots.

### 3.2 Coupling Team Predictions
Visual, state, and action tokens across all robots are fed into a single Transformer and interact densely through cross-agent attention. In handover tasks where one robot's move directly triggers another, actions are computed while factoring in the partner's intent and anticipated visual changes. Flow matching is used as the training objective to supervise both future visual latents and action vectors simultaneously.

### 3.3 Preserving Per-Robot Interfaces
Mixing all tokens risks confusion about which camera belongs to whom and whose arm should move. The model prevents this through several mechanisms:
- Regular-simplex rotary position embeddings: Assigns equidistant geometric codes to each robot, shared across all onboard camera views of that robot.
- Action-to-video bias: Adds the mean of each robot's action tokens to the future visual tokens of its own cameras, directly coupling control with visual prediction.
- Task-role embeddings: Decouples individual agent identity from task roles (such as holding a camera vs. handing over an object). This prevents control confusion even if two robots share similar roles.

### 3.4 Two-Stage Training and Closed-Loop Control
To leverage a pretrained single-robot backbone (GR00T 2), training proceeds in two stages:
1. Warm-up: Adapts to individual robot cameras and control interfaces.
2. Team training: Uses synchronized multi-robot data with cross-agent attention and randomized agent ID shuffling to master coordination.
During deployment, the first 8 of the 24 generated steps are executed synchronously in closed loop before replanning from fresh observations.

(c) Joint supervision of video and actions via flow matching. (d) At inference time, actions for all robots are jointly generated, and the first 8 steps are executed.

sections.heading: Outstanding coordination across two real robots and up to four simulated arms
sections.summary: MAWAM achieved a 67.8% average success rate across three real-world tasks using only six onboard views, outperforming baselines. It also reached 90.3% across eight simulation tasks, with ablations proving the necessity of future prediction and cross-agent attention.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Real-Robot Coordinated Manipulation
Evaluations were conducted on two Galaxea R1 Pro bimanual mobile robots across three tasks: laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover. No static overhead cameras were used; inputs were restricted to six onboard cameras mounted on the robots' heads and wrists.
- Results: MAWAM achieved a 67.8% average success rate across the three tasks, significantly outperforming MA-VLA (48.9%), CLS-DP (37.8%), and GauDP (28.9%). In laundry-bag collection, where robots must continuously hold the bag open together, MAWAM reached 53.3% versus MA-VLA's 30.0%.

### 4.2 Simulation (Eight Tasks with 2 to 4 Arms)
MAWAM was evaluated across all eight tasks in the RoboFactory benchmark using 2 to 4 Panda arms, achieving an overall average success rate of 90.3%. It maintained high performance as arm counts increased, reaching 95.0% on the four-arm relay task Long Pipeline Delivery and 97.0% on the joint photography task Take Photo.

### 4.3 Ablation Studies: What Makes It Work?
Ablating individual components revealed key insights:
- Removing cross-agent attention: Severing cross-agent attention dropped four-arm relay success from 95.0% to 39.0% (and real-robot average from 67.8% to 52.2%).
- Robustness to teammate delays: When one robot was intentionally paused for 16 steps during a relay, MAWAM automatically delayed the receiving robot by a median of 12 steps to maintain synchronization, preserving a 99% success rate (compared to 44% for the uncoordinated baseline).
- Removing future video supervision: Dropping the video loss during team training caused Place Food (where one robot places items while another holds a lid open) to plunge from 78.0% to 47.0%. Learning visual future prediction is critical for precise coordination involving stationary holding.
- Future tokens at test time: While skipping future video denoising during inference preserved action quality, completely removing future tokens from the sequence dropped relay success to 0%, showing that future tokens serve as a computational scratchpad.
- Roles and regular-simplex IDs: Omitting task roles dropped Place Food success to 0%. Furthermore, regular-simplex IDs with random shuffling generalized significantly better than fixed slot IDs.

sections.heading: A new world-model foundation for multi-agent coordination
sections.summary: This section summarizes MAWAM's effectiveness in unifying action generation with future visual prediction, concluding that anticipating physical futures is vital for coordinated manipulation.
sections.details:
When a robot team operates in the physical world, each robot's movements shape the future environment in which its teammates must act. MAWAM models this fundamental interdependence by jointly generating the entire team's continuous actions and future camera views in a single sample.

In real-robot settings without external overhead cameras—relying solely on onboard views—MAWAM achieved a 67.8% average success rate, outperforming MA-VLA by 18.9 percentage points. It also achieved an impressive 90.3% success rate in simulation. Ablations confirmed that cross-agent attention and future-video supervision are decisive factors for coordination, proving that the world-action model framework is highly practical for multi-robot teams sharing a physical space.

sections.heading: Current limitations and the path toward human-robot collaboration
sections.summary: This section outlines current constraints regarding fixed teams of up to four arms, and discusses future directions such as dynamic team compositions, heterogeneous robots, and human-robot teaming.
sections.details:
Experiments in this work were limited to fixed teams of up to four robots. While inference time scaled favorably—increasing only modestly from 1.40 seconds for two arms to 1.85 seconds for four arms—scaling to much larger teams remains an open challenge.

Future work should also address dynamic team compositions where members enter or leave mid-task, as well as heterogeneous teams with diverse robot embodiments and sensor suites. Furthermore, the future visual predictions and actions generated by MAWAM can provide interpretability, helping humans intuitively understand what the team plans to do next. Integrating human partners into the prediction loop holds exciting potential for seamless human-robot physical collaboration.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details, coordinate routing, and video accuracy
sections.summary: Supplementary details cover real-world and simulation setups, view and control routing rules, the geometric properties of regular-simplex embeddings, and quantitative video prediction benchmarks.
sections.details:
The appendix provides detailed implementation and experimental setups that support the main text:

- View and control routing: Robot cameras and control dimensions are strictly managed via explicit metadata and selection matrices. On real hardware, each robot operates three cameras (left head and both wrists) and a 16-DoF logical action space (relative end-effector poses and gripper openings for both arms), totaling a 32-dimensional action space across the pair.
- Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) allocation: In addition to time, height, and width, an agent axis is added to the attention heads. Pretrained low-frequency components are assigned to agent identification, utilizing 4-vertex regular-simplex coordinates to provide equidistant rotation angles, ensuring order-invariant geometric discriminability.
- Quantitative video accuracy: Future frame accuracy was evaluated using PSNR. When excluding static backgrounds and evaluating regions where more than 5% of pixels move, MAWAM achieved 4 to 7 dB higher PSNR compared to a baseline that simply copies the last observed frame, confirming that physical motion is faithfully anticipated.

takeaways: In coordinated multi-robot control, jointly denoising teammate actions alongside the shared visual future within a single Transformer is remarkably effective.
Even without denoising future video pixels to completion at test time, retaining future tokens in the latent space preserves control performance by acting as a computational scratchpad.
When adapting single-robot foundation backbones to multi-robot setups, inserting an individual-robot warm-up stage before joint team training dramatically stabilizes learning.
Strictly separating agent identity (regular-simplex embeddings) from functional assignments (role embeddings) is key to preventing command confusion.
limitations: Evaluations are currently limited to fixed team structures of up to four arms and two identical robots, without support for dynamically changing team sizes.

In real-time deployment, the system is constrained by closed-loop replanning cycles (around 0.3 to 0.5 s) and communication latencies, limiting responsiveness to millisecond-level high-frequency contact dynamics.
Validation on heterogeneous teams featuring varied robot embodiments and sensor configurations remains an open topic for future research.
